query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a controlled minor amount of aluminum during DED processing will induce a γ + γ′ dual‐phase microstructure in a titanium–nickel primary high-entropy alloy, thereby enhancing its elevated-temperature mechanical properties relative to the same alloy produced without aluminum.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy in which titanium and nickel are the primary constituents, produced via DED with a single-phase (FCC or BCC) solid solution structure.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled aluminum addition (e.g., approximately 5–10 at%) into the Ti–Ni primary HEA during the DED manufacturing process.
generation.conditions: The alloy composition must adhere to the HEA definition (each element within 5–35 at%), with processing and testing performed under identical DED parameters and operating temperatures (e.g., above 700 °C, but below limits where unwanted phase transformations occur).
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a dual-phase microstructure featuring a disordered γ matrix coupled with ordered γ′ precipitates.
generation.mechanism: Aluminum promotes the nucleation of the ordered γ′ phase, which acts to impede dislocation motion and stabilize the microstructure at elevated temperatures, resulting in improved creep resistance and tensile strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: The aluminum-modified alloy is expected to exhibit higher elevated-temperature tensile strength and creep resistance compared to the single-phase Ti–Ni HEA without Al addition.
generation.baseline: Performance benchmarks of the same Ti–Ni primary HEA produced under identical DED conditions but without the aluminum addition.
generation.boundary: The improvement is anticipated within operating temperatures above approximately 700 °C and within the compositional boundaries of HEAs (all elements between 5–35 at%), provided the aluminum content is controlled to avoid deleterious phases.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of property enhancement is uncertain without direct experimental data; additionally, potential trade-offs in ductility or toughness may arise if the dual-phase balance is not optimally maintained.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two sets of Ti–Ni primary HEAs via DED processing: one set with a controlled aluminum addition (5–10 at%) and a control set without aluminum. Subject both sets to identical heat-treatment protocols and test them at elevated temperatures (e.g., 800 °C). Conduct mechanical testing (tensile and creep tests) and microstructural characterization (using SEM/TEM) to verify the formation of the dual-phase microstructure.
measurements: Microstructural phase analysis (confirmation of γ + γ′ dual-phase formation)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aluminum-containing alloy fails to form the predicted γ + γ′ dual-phase microstructure or does not show a statistically significant improvement in tensile strength and creep resistance at elevated temperatures relative to the control, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: With the development of high-temperature metallic materials, Ni-based superalloys have been unable to meet the requirements of aerospace engines. It is urgent to find a new high-performance alloy to replace the Ni-based superalloy []. Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) based on refractory elements with superior high-temperature mechanical properties have recently attracted intensive research attention, which are regarded as promising candidates for high-temperature structural materials [,,]. However, their inferior plasticity along with high ductile–brittle transition temperature and high density seriously limits their aerospace applications, where the requirements are mainly focus on the deformability and high specific strength of alloys.

The discovery of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) by Yeh et al. has promoted the development of new concepts and fresh perspectives on alloy design within the emerging era of HEAs.− HEAs consist of five or more principal elements with equal or nearly equal atomic ratios and form single-phase solid solutions. The concentration of each element in HEA typically lies in the range of 5–35 atom %;, however, some HEAs may also contain minor elements with concentrations below 5 atom %. In equimolar HEAs, each element has an equal probability of occupying lattice sites in the crystal structure. In the 21st century, HEAs stand out as a novel material with numerous benefits. These alloys offer notable advantages, including outstanding resistance to corrosion and oxidation, along with impressive mechanical properties. Films made from high-entropy alloys (HEAs) showcase these favorable properties while often presenting lower material costs compared to their bulk counterparts. This makes HEA films an economically attractive option for various applications. The synthesis phenomena for thin-film composition design of HEAs are similar to those of bulk HEAs. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are defined as alloys that are composed of more than 4 elements with near equi-atomic percentage [,,,]. Due to their high mixing entropy, HEAs tend to form simple solid-solution phases, such as face-centered-cubic (FCC) [,], body-centered-cubic (BCC) [,,], and hexagonal-close-packed (HCP) structures [,]. With the entropic stabilization of solid-solution phases, HEAs have attracted significant attention, because of their outstanding properties at elevated temperatures, which results from severe lattice distortion and microstructural stability at high temperatures [,,]. Many refractory HEAs (RHEAs), which mainly consist of BCC-type single solid-solution phase, have been developed and investigated due to their excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures []. The excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures in RHEAs are significantly associated with their unique atomic structures (distorted lattices) and high melting temperatures of the constitutive refractory elements (Ti, Nb, V, Mo, Ta, W, and Cr) [,,,]. reading.lever: Incorporate a controlled aluminum addition via DED processing to induce a γ + γ′ dual-phase microstructure in a Ti–Ni primary HEA.
reading.why: This approach leverages proven enhancement of thermal stability and strength from aluminum-induced dual-phase formation in related systems, directly targeting elevated-temperature limitations in Ti–Ni primary alloys.
